opus-5.5.text:
Well, picking up an egg intact is hard, don't get me wrong. You need a gentle enough grasp that you don't crush it, and robots have historically been pretty clumsy. But cracking an egg is a different level of difficulty, and I think it shows how far we still have to go.

When you crack an egg, you have to apply just the right amount of force, enough to fracture the shell but not so much that you smash it and get shell fragments everywhere. Then you have to get your thumbs into that crack and pull the two halves apart, so the contents fall cleanly into the bowl without the yolk breaking. You're dealing with a brittle shell that fractures unpredictably, and a liquid interior that sloshes and flows. All of that happens in a fraction of a second, and much of it depends on subtle tactile feedback that we're not even consciously aware of.

That's the essence of Moravec's paradox. The things we find hard, like chess, Go, or calculus, turn out to be relatively easy for computers. The things a small child can do without thinking, like cracking an egg, folding a towel, or clearing a dinner table, are incredibly hard for robots. We take them for granted because evolution has spent hundreds of millions of years refining our sensorimotor skills.

The underlying problem is uncertainty. A robot doesn't know the exact friction of the surface, the precise mass distribution, or how the material will deform or break. Tiny errors in perception and control compound, and the physics of contact is notoriously hard to model. The egg is a nice example because you can't fully simulate it, and you can't easily collect millions of real examples either, since every attempt makes a mess.

So when people see videos of humanoid robots doing backflips and assume we're a year or two away from robots doing all our household chores, I like to bring up the egg. Dexterous manipulation is still very much an open problem. We're making real progress, but I think it's important to be honest about how hard this is.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, picking up an egg intact is actually something we've gotten reasonably good at. You can do it with a soft gripper, or with suction, and you can be fairly conservative about it — you just need to not squeeze too hard, and if you're careful about the geometry you'll succeed most of the time. It's a bounded problem.

Cracking an egg is a completely different animal. Think about what's involved. You have to grip it firmly enough to control it, strike it against an edge with just the right amount of force — too little and nothing happens, too much and you've got shell fragments in the bowl. Then you have to pull the two halves apart in a coordinated way so the contents come out cleanly, and the membrane doesn't tear in the wrong place, and you don't end up with yolk on the counter. And every egg is a little different. The shell thickness varies, the size varies, the way the fracture propagates is essentially unpredictable.

So you're dealing with a deformable, fragile object that changes state in the middle of the task. It goes from a rigid shell to a broken shell to a liquid you're trying to direct. That's what we call a contact-rich manipulation problem, and it's exactly the kind of thing that's humbling for robots. Humans do it without thinking — a kid can learn it in an afternoon — but it draws on this enormous reservoir of tactile intuition that we really don't know how to give a machine yet.

That's why I pay attention to it. It's a very ordinary task that exposes how much of the physical world we still can't model, and how much of dexterity is really about responding to things you couldn't predict.

r001.rationale: The response says intact eggs can be picked up with soft grippers or suction and by avoiding excessive force, but it does not explain that eggs strongly resist cracking under squeezing.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a roughly one-millimetre contact-position error determining whether an object is held or dropped.

astra-6.text:
Well, picking up an egg is already a challenge, because you have to grasp it firmly enough that it doesn’t slip, but gently enough that you don’t break it. But cracking an egg means deliberately breaking it—and controlling how it breaks. You have to strike it with the right amount of force, open the shell, and get the contents out without dropping pieces of shell into the bowl.

And the egg changes as you do this. You go from manipulating a solid object to handling a broken shell and this slippery, deformable material inside. You can’t just execute a fixed sequence of motions; you have to respond to what actually happens.

Humans do that so casually that we forget how much skill is involved. That’s why I find it so impressive: it brings together perception, dexterity, and dealing with uncertainty in a very ordinary kitchen task.

sol-6.1.text:
Picking up an egg is a challenge, but you’re trying to preserve the object. Cracking it means deliberately changing it, and doing that in a very controlled way. You have to apply enough force to break the shell, but not so much that you crush it, and then separate the shell while letting the contents fall out. The material changes as you act on it, so you have to respond to what actually happens.

That’s what makes it so interesting to me. Something we do almost without thinking turns out to involve this extraordinary combination of sensing, dexterity, and adaptation.
